THE TRADITION OF SEARCH - STUDY NOTES (Section A: The Search for Meaning and Values)

LEARNING OUTCOMES
- Define philosophy and explain its nature and purpose in the search for meaning and values.
- Summarise two main ideas each of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle and why each was important.
- Outline the place of the Sophists in ancient Greek society and their importance.
- Identify and explain three key moments in philosophy from classical to contemporary times.

KEY TERMS
- Rhetoric: the use of language to influence or persuade.
- Relativism: the view that there is no absolute or objective truth.
- Virtue: a moral good.
- Metaphysics: branch of philosophy that explores the abstract and non-physical.
- Nihilism: the belief that nothing truly exists or that all values are worthless.
- Hedonism: the belief that pursuing pleasure or avoiding pain is the way to achieve the ultimate good.
- Empiricism: the position that perceiving something through the senses is the test of its truth.
- Allegory: a story in which abstract ideas are represented by characters or events.

WHAT IS PHILOSOPHY?
- 2018: Dublin's 3Arena (seats up to 9,000) was full for a debate between Canadian psychologist Dr Jordan B. Peterson (12 Rules for Life, Beyond Order) and atheist author Sam Harris (Free Will, Lying) on morality, the greatest good and whether values can work outside religion.
- Philosophy means "the love of wisdom", from Greek philos (love) and sophos (wisdom).
- It lets us step back from everyday concerns to examine how the world works and how it might work better; gives tools for thinking about big questions.
- It examines existence, knowledge, love and the best way to live. Can be as complex as maths or as simple as a joke.
- Usually abstract (ideas, not concrete reality), done through reflection. Unlike science (results, experiment, verifiable data), it pursues knowledge for its own sake.
- Aristotle: "Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom." Steve Jobs: "I would trade all of my technology for an afternoon with Socrates."

HOW PHILOSOPHY WORKS
- It is about asking questions, building on children's natural curiosity.
- Before answering big questions (meaning of life, suffering) we must examine what the questions and terms mean.
- It challenges preconceptions (beliefs not properly considered) through reflection (thinking) and argument (looking at an idea from all angles).
- Example: Plato's Republic (about 375 BCE) - someone says returning what you borrowed is always moral. Socrates refutes this: returning weapons to a friend who has become dangerously insane is not moral. Stripping away preconceptions brings us closer to universal truths.

PHILOSOPHY AND THE SEARCH FOR MEANING
- Online searches give instant information, but questions that really matter need deep thought.
- Philosophy gives a framework for our thoughts, drawing on 2,500 years of great thinkers; it strengthens our thinking and helps us decide how best to live.

THE SOPHISTS IN ANCIENT GREEK SOCIETY
- Fifth-century Athens: Athenians helped drive Persian invaders out in 479 BCE, bringing prosperity. Athens flourished under the general Pericles: rebuilding of the Parthenon, sculptures of Phidias, tragedies of Sophocles.
- Athens was a democracy: free citizens ran the state; judges and officials were chosen by lot (like modern juries).
- To succeed in public life you had to be well educated; those with money could be trained by the Sophists.
- "Sophist" roughly equals "professor". They came from different parts of Greece, seen as wise and well travelled, and taught courses for a fee in major cities.
- Subjects: poetry, grammar, mythology, religion, literature, statesmanship, generalship - but the key skill was rhetoric, needed for politics or law.

SOPHIST BELIEFS
- Not seekers of truth; focused on the person and their place in the world.
- Taught students to argue both sides equally fiercely, whether they agreed or not; rhetoric was only to win debates.
- Taught how to win lawsuits (good money). Reputation for dishonesty and cynicism (assuming people act from selfish motives). Accused of letting truth or goodness be abandoned if it did not suit those in power.
- Protagoras and Gorgias: truth is relative (relativism). Example: one person says it is hot, the other says it is not - both are true for the Sophists.
- Protagoras: "Man is the measure of all things." Truth became closer to opinion than fact, contributing to moral breakdown.
- Gorgias: no way to tell knowledge from opinion; we filter everything through our own thoughts and words.
- Thrasymachus: "justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger."
- Sophists charged highly, so only the wealthy benefited - creating social and economic division. Could "strongest" mean wealthiest? Is that still true today?
- Francis Bacon: "'What is truth?' said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer."

IMPORTANCE OF THE SOPHISTS
- People became the focus of thought: pre-Socratic philosophers such as Thales and Heraclitus asked about the natural world (how the universe began, what it is made of). The Sophists shifted the focus to the human person - crucial for philosophy; later philosophers put human experience at the centre.
- Importance of debate: theories must be challenged and critically examined. This reaches its greatest expression in Plato's dialogues. Seen today in the justice system (prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; defence casts doubt on evidence). Problem: if there is no truth and the best arguer wins, is that just?
- Legacy: traditionalists suspected them of caring more about money; pupils admired their sceptical, questioning attitude. Their ideas were seen as dangerous. Criticised by Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. Today "sophist" means someone who argues to win without believing what they say.

SOCRATES, PLATO AND ARISTOTLE
- Lived in a roughly 150-year period in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, working mostly in Athens. Plato was Socrates' pupil and taught Aristotle.

SOCRATES
- Born around 470 BCE in Athens. Wrote nothing; known from his pupils Plato (philosopher) and Xenophon (historian), and the comic playwright Aristophanes.
- Physically tough former soldier; went barefoot in all weather, same clothes all year. Plato said he looked like a satyr or the god Silenus; Aristophanes mocked him for "strutting like a waterfowl".
- A ceaseless questioner: used questions to expose gaps in reasoning and get nearer the truth. "The unexamined life is not worth living."
- 399 BCE: sentenced to death for rejecting the city's gods and corrupting its youth.

SOCRATES' FIRST IDEA: SOCRATIC IGNORANCE
- At his trial he distinguished himself from the Sophists: he did not claim their vast wisdom.
- Most people think they know more than they do; his only wisdom was knowing how little he knew.
- He asked "innocent" questions of so-called experts to expose their lack of knowledge.
- Importance: great thinkers question their assumptions before forming a theory. Later example: Rene Descartes' "method of doubt".

SOCRATES' SECOND IDEA: VIRTUE AND CARE FOR THE SOUL
- We must care for the soul above all; Athenians cared for wealth, status and bodies but neglected the soul.
- Wealth, beauty or strength cannot create virtue, but virtue creates all things truly beneficial.
- All virtue is knowledge: knowing what is right means doing what is right; wrongdoing comes from ignorance.
- "The really important thing is not to live but to live well."
- Only one true virtue: insight into what truly benefits humankind and nourishes the soul. Wisdom is the key to a virtuous life and saving the soul.
- Against the Sophists (strongest argument wins; you are right if you believe you are; justice is the interest of the strongest), Socrates said what pleases us is not necessarily good; we must act for the common good.
- Never permissible to do wrong, even if wronged (e.g. wrong to escape prison even if the charge was unjust).
- Wanted a universal definition of justice, against Sophist relativism; our duty to explore justice/injustice, right/wrong, courage/cowardice.
- Virtue is necessary for happiness. Distinguished happiness from pleasure: pleasure is good, but true pleasure and lasting happiness come only through a virtuous life.
- Importance: first to seriously consider virtue; Aristotle and the Roman Stoics started from him. Alasdair MacIntyre's book After Virtue shows virtue is still a major concern.

PLATO
- Empiricism and illusions: the Ames window and the Penrose triangle show senses can deceive. ("Your eyes can deceive you; don't trust them" - Obi-Wan Kenobi.)
- Born in Athens around 428 BCE, just after Pericles' death; aristocratic family involved in politics.
- Studied under Socrates; greatly affected by his trial and death; left Athens to travel through Greece, Italy and Egypt.
- Returned around age fifty and founded the Academy - forerunner of the modern university (origin of "academic"); excellent in study and research, attracting mathematicians too. Most famous pupil: Aristotle (twenty years there).
- About twenty-seven genuine dialogues survive. His system covers ethics, morals, politics, art and epistemology (study of knowledge).
- Believed true knowledge comes through the mind alone, not the physical senses.

PLATO'S FIRST IDEA: THE THEORY OF IDEAL FORMS
- Things in our world take their qualities from an "ideal form" that exists independently (sweetness, saltiness, justice, "chair-ness", "wall-ness").
- The ideal form is more real than the physical object because it never changes, erodes or is destroyed.
- Example: the International Prototype of the Kilogram (IPK, "Big K") - a golf-ball-sized platinum and iridium cylinder kept under three bell jars in a triple-locked vault in Sevres, France. It lost almost 50 milligrams over 130 years. In 2018 the kilogram was redefined using Planck's constant, a standard in nature - closer to an ideal form.
- Allegory of the cave: prisoners chained facing a wall see only shadows of puppet-like figures cast by a fire and think the shadows are real. A freed prisoner is dazzled by the fire and blinded by the sun; if he returns to tell the others, they do not believe him or are angry.
- Meaning: the physical world known through the senses is the world of shadows; the sun is the ultimate ideal form - the good. Our world of change, ageing and decay is less real than the eternal ideal world. Truth, beauty, goodness and justice are unchanging ideal forms.
- William Blake: "Man has closed himself up, till he sees all things through narrow chinks of his cavern."
- Films: Enchanted, The Smurfs (comic), The Matrix (questioning). In The Matrix, Cypher eats steak in the virtual world knowing it is not real; he represents unenlightened prisoners who prefer comfortable illusion to harsh reality.
- Legacy: Aristotle influenced but disagreed about forms being more real. Neoplatonists (third century CE) revived ideal forms: mind before matter, ideal before physical. They influenced St Basil the Great, St Gregory Nazianzen and St Augustine.

PLATO'S SECOND IDEA: AN ULTIMATE GOOD
- The aim of his philosophy: the summum bonum - the supreme good from which all others come; achieving it brings true happiness.
- Dialogue Philebus: the Sophist Protarchus says the highest good is physical pleasure; Socrates says pure pleasure without thought suits only an oyster, and the highest good is wisdom. Plato's view: a sensible mix of pleasure and wisdom, led by knowledge and reason.
- Dialogue Phaedrus - allegory of the chariot (the soul): a dark horse (physical appetites and desires), a white horse (spirit straining for victory and virtue), and the charioteer (reason) who makes them work together towards a goal - neither ignoring nor letting them run amok.
- Legacy: Neoplatonists - all things come from and aim at the good. St Thomas Aquinas - God is creator and the end to which humans direct themselves. Against: Friedrich Nietzsche's nihilism - all values arbitrary. Robert Nozick (twentieth century) - people would reject a life of artificially induced pleasure (backing Plato against hedonism).

ARISTOTLE
- Born 384 BCE at Stageira in Thrace (north of Greece), under growing Macedonian control. Father was physician to King Amyntas II of Macedonia.
- At about seventeen went to Plato's Academy; stayed over twenty years as pupil and teacher; devoted friend of Plato.
- After Plato's death his ideas diverged. Tutored the future Alexander the Great for King Philip II. Returned to Athens in 335 or 334 BCE and founded the Lyceum. Died in Chalcis aged sixty-three. Thin, well dressed, elegant hair and many rings.
- Founding father of natural sciences (biology, zoology); "father of Western logic" - formal system of reasoning. Wrote on maths, biology, politics, ethics, literary criticism.

ARISTOTLE'S FIRST IDEA: SUBSTANTIAL FORMS
- Did not fully reject forms, but denied they exist independently in an abstract, unknowable way.
- The individual real object truly exists; forms exist because we observe them in real objects.
- Substantial form: a form that cannot change without the object changing its nature.
- Accidental form: a surface attribute that does not affect the essentials.
- Example: a round, white stone. For Plato, roundness, whiteness and stone-ness are more real. For Aristotle they exist only in real things. Painting it red is an accidental change; becoming square, black and spongy would be substantial.
- Influence: scholastic philosophers, mainly St Thomas Aquinas (commentaries on matter and form) and Francisco Suarez. Rene Descartes (17th century) tried to replace it with a "mechanistic" explanation: nature works by mechanical laws; objects are "extension" (length, breadth, depth) and "mode" (shape).
- Raphael's fresco The School of Athens (Apostolic Palace, Vatican): Plato points up to the heavens (abstract, ideal); Aristotle gestures out to the world (empirical, practical). But there was also much continuity.

ARISTOTLE'S SECOND IDEA: FIRST CAUSE AND UNMOVED MOVER
- In Metaphysics he argues for a "first cause" of being, identified as God.
- Everything changes and perishes, so there must be an unchanging, imperishable unmoved mover setting all in motion.
- It cannot be physical (kicking a ball changes you too), so it must be immaterial. God is pure thought - "thought of thought".
- God moves things not by causing them but as an inspiration or goal - the ultimate good. God moves by being loved (like a magnet drawing metal without touching it).
- Differences from the Christian God: the unmoved mover has no thought for things outside himself, no divine plan, is not involved in people's lives, and friendship with God is impossible.
- Importance: an ordered universe set in motion by an intelligent being refuted Sophist relativism; influenced Neoplatonists such as Plotinus and Christian philosophers such as St Thomas Aquinas.

AFTER THE GREEKS
- Metaphysics gave way to practical philosophies in Rome: Epicureanism and Stoicism (techniques for living well).
- As Rome declined: Cynics (wandering preachers criticising Roman moral depravity) and Sceptics (relativists: certainty impossible; follow your instincts).

KEY MOMENT 1: MEDIEVAL CHRISTIAN PHILOSOPHERS
- Christians were persecuted for nearly 300 years; worst under Emperor Diocletian (303-311 CE). Constantine converted and sponsored Christianity.
- Plotinus (204-270 CE): first Neoplatonist; Neoplatonism was the background for medieval Christian philosophy.

ST AUGUSTINE
- Born 354 CE in Thagaste, Roman Africa (now Souk Ahras, Algeria). Mother a devout Christian.
- Influenced by Manichaeism - a strict (ascetic) form of Gnosticism, seeing physical things as evil and spirit as good.
- Before thirty moved to Milan; converted to Christianity through Bishop Ambrose and Neoplatonist-influenced Christians. Became Bishop of Hippo (near Annaba, Algeria).
- Philosophy formed by Christian faith and Neoplatonism: the physical world has a spiritual dimension; humans have free will.
- Confessions: all humans are on a spiritual journey driven by a desire for happiness. "You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You." Restlessness is needed to start the search for God; pride and despair can block this longing.
- Love: Plato's followers saw love as desire to possess the beauty or virtue of the beloved. For Augustine, receiving God's love makes it possible to love others. After a friend's death he wrote that real love overcomes death because it is rooted in God: "Blessed be he who loves You, and his friend in You, and his enemy for Your sake..." (4:9). Christian love extends to enemies.
- Other famous work: The City of God.

ST THOMAS AQUINAS (1225-1274)
- Monasteries had become great centres of learning; universities of Oxford, Paris and Bologna were being founded.
- Wrote over eighty books: Summa contra Gentiles (philosophical summary of Christianity); Summa Theologiae (ordered theology); Questiones Disputate (questions and answers from discussions with students).
- Bishop Robert Barron (a contemporary Thomist): Aquinas' influence "has been so massive that it's difficult even to get a grip on it".
- Born near Aquino between Rome and Naples; parents were feudal landowners hoping he would be a prosperous abbot, but he became a mendicant (poor) Dominican friar. Studied at the Dominican University in Paris where he met Aristotle's philosophy, recently rediscovered by Arab scholars.
- Society moved from feudal farming to urban trade; Aristotle's practical philosophy suited it.
- Aristotle and Aquinas: the universe is ordered with a plan; the search for meaning is only possible in an ordered universe.
- Combined Aristotle with Christian revelation (unlike Augustine's Platonism). Reason can work within faith: start with faith, use reason to reach conclusions - controversial then, a major shift.
- Happiness: all human actions pursue goals; all are "subgoals" of an ultimate goal. He rejected wealth, honours, glory, power and physical pleasure as ultimate goals. Only God, the complete good, satisfies; a virtuous life is the road to the contemplation of God.
- Jordan B. Peterson: "Aim at something. Pick the best target you can currently conceptualise."

KEY MOMENT 2: THE AGE OF REASON (17TH CENTURY)
- Thinkers broke from Plato and relied on observation - reasoning from first principles or inductive reasoning.
- Background: Humanists (14th-15th centuries) re-examined classical writings, promoting virtue, rhetoric, history, poetry; a more human-focused view (many were devout Christians). The Renaissance showed the human form boldly (e.g. Brunelleschi's dome of Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence).
- Astronomers challenged Ptolemy's earth-centred universe (accepted since the second century).
- Printing press and moveable type spread ideas fast and helped the Protestant Reformation.
- Reformation: highlighted corrupt practices later addressed by the Council of Trent (1545-1563). Martin Luther (1483-1546), John Calvin and Huldrych Zwingli; returning to first principles in religion; rejecting traditions not supported by scripture. Each person interpreting scripture led to individualism in faith and division in the Western Church.

RENE DESCARTES (1596-1650)
- Born near Tours, France; father a lawyer. Studied at the Jesuit College in Anjou. Gifted mathematician and scientist; "father of modern philosophy". Interested in human existence; wanted a sure foundation for philosophy against growing scepticism.
- Method of doubt: reject everything in a proposition that can be doubted; what remains is objectively true. He even doubted the senses and mathematics using the "evil demon" idea.
- Example: sitting by the fire - he might be dreaming, or tricked by an all-powerful evil demon. Can he prove he exists?
- The Truman Show: producer Christoff (Ed Harris) is like the evil demon, keeping Truman in a fake reality TV world; only when Truman doubts does he near the truth.
- Conclusion: he cannot doubt that he is doubting. "We cannot doubt of our existence while we doubt." Doubting is thinking, so he is a thinking thing: "I think, therefore I am" (Cogito, ergo sum). This rational view of humans as thinkers marks the Age of Reason.
- The Age of Reason led to the Enlightenment (Voltaire, Diderot; Isaac Newton's laws of gravity; Benjamin Franklin's electricity experiments).

KEY MOMENT 3: ROMANTICISM AND EXISTENTIALISM
- Many 18th-century artists and thinkers found the focus on the rational and measurable stifling; they wanted freedom beyond planned logic.
- Descartes saw an old winding town as poorly planned and to be rebuilt; Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-1778) found it magical and poetic. This attitude is Romanticism.
- Closely tied to the arts: Wagner's operas, Byron's poems, Caspar David Friedrich's paintings; mythical, magical and transcendental (spiritual) subjects returned. William Blake (1757-1827) is typical.
- Values passion, emotion, self-expression; the "tortured artist"; highly subjective; the individual as heroic outcast.
- Influenced existentialism: human identity is supremely important; humans are masters of their own destiny. First existentialist: Danish philosopher Soren Kierkegaard (1813-1855).

FRIEDRICH NIETZSCHE (born 1844)
- Both Romantic and existentialist. Born near Leipzig, Germany. Father (a Lutheran pastor) and older brother died in his childhood. Studied theology, then philology (study of language). Professor of Greek at the University of Basel by twenty-four.
- Early Romantic phase: close friend of composer Richard Wagner (a substitute father; Romantic genius with fiery temper).
- The Birth of Tragedy: championed the wild Greek god Dionysus over Christianity, which he said rejects life on Earth for the afterlife.
- Late 1870s: quarrelled with Wagner, broke with Romanticism; then a nervous breakdown; ten years trying to recover while writing.
- Used shock to wake people from complacency (self-satisfaction with lack of awareness).
- "God is dead" and we are responsible: without a supreme authority, humans must create their own values.
- Mature works: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil - focus on values.
- Superman (Ubermensch): a new breed of human beyond ordinary limits; Christian morality and national laws do not bind him. Religion, democracy and patriotism are for the weak. Ordinary humanity is a stepping stone between animal and superman.
- Eternal recurrence: all events repeat forever, so live every moment fully so it would be no burden to live again. Only the superman has the will to endure it.

rows.prompt: Give a brief definition of philosophy and explain its purpose in the search for meaning.
rows.model_answer: Philosophy means 'the love of wisdom'. It uses reflection and argument to ask big questions about existence, knowledge, love and the best way to live. It gives us a framework for our thoughts and the tools to think clearly about how to live.

rows.prompt: Explain what the Sophists meant by relativism, with an example.
rows.model_answer: Relativism is the view that there is no absolute or objective truth; truth depends on each person's experience. If one person says it is hot and another says it is not, both are speaking the truth. Protagoras said 'Man is the measure of all things'.

rows.prompt: Name two ways the Sophists contributed to the development of philosophy.
rows.model_answer: They shifted the focus of philosophy from the natural world to the human person and their place in the world. They also taught that theories must be challenged and debated critically, which reached its greatest expression in Plato's dialogues and is seen today in the justice system.

rows.prompt: Explain Socrates' teaching on virtue and care for the soul.
rows.model_answer: Socrates said we must care for the soul above wealth, status or the body. He believed virtue is knowledge: whoever knows what is right will do it, and wrongdoing comes from ignorance. True happiness comes only through a virtuous life.

rows.prompt: Describe Plato's allegory of the cave and what it illustrates.
rows.model_answer: Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on a wall and think they are real. A prisoner who escapes is dazzled by the fire and the sun, and when he returns the others do not believe him. It shows our physical world is a world of shadows, and the sun represents the ultimate good.

rows.prompt: Explain Aristotle's idea of substantial forms.
rows.model_answer: For Aristotle, forms exist only in real objects, not independently. A substantial form cannot be changed without the object changing its nature, while an accidental form is a surface feature. Painting a white stone red is accidental; making it square, black and spongy would be substantial.

rows.prompt: What did Thomas Aquinas teach about human happiness?
rows.model_answer: Aquinas said all human actions pursue goals, and these are subgoals of one ultimate goal. Wealth, honours, glory, power and pleasure cannot satisfy us. Only God, the complete good, can, and a virtuous life is the road to contemplating God.

rows.prompt: What did Nietzsche mean by 'God is dead' and the 'superman'?
rows.model_answer: Nietzsche said God is dead and humans are responsible, so without a supreme authority people must create their own values. His superman (Ubermensch) is a new human beyond ordinary limits, not bound by Christian morality or national laws. He saw ordinary humanity as a stepping stone to the superman.

rows.prompt: Outline the place of the Sophists in the society of ancient Greece and their importance in the development of philosophy. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: In fifth-century Athens, after the Persians were driven out in 479 BCE and the city flourished under Pericles, Athens was a democracy where citizens ran the state. To succeed in public life, people had to be well educated and able to speak well. The Sophists, whose name roughly means 'professor', were wise, well-travelled teachers who charged high fees to teach grammar, poetry, mythology and above all rhetoric. They were not seekers of truth; they taught students to argue both sides to win debates and lawsuits. Protagoras said 'Man is the measure of all things', meaning truth is relative, and Thrasymachus said 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger'. This contributed to moral breakdown and their fees created social division. Yet they were important for philosophy. First, they shifted the focus from the natural world, studied by pre-Socratics like Thales and Heraclitus, to the human person; later philosophers kept human experience at the centre. Second, they taught that theories must be challenged and debated, which found its greatest expression in Plato's dialogues and is still seen in our justice system.
rows.marking_scheme: Place in society (up to 8): Athenian democracy, need for education, paid travelling teachers, rhetoric, winning debates/lawsuits, relativism (Protagoras, Gorgias), Thrasymachus, reputation for dishonesty, division. Importance (up to 12): focus on human person vs pre-Socratics; importance of debate and critique; influence on Plato's dialogues; justice system; legacy and criticism by Socrates, Plato, Aristotle.

rows.prompt: Examine the influence of two of Socrates' ideas on the development of philosophy. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Socrates was a ceaseless questioner who said 'the unexamined life is not worth living'. His first idea was Socratic ignorance. Unlike the Sophists, he did not claim great wisdom; he believed most people think they know more than they do, and his only wisdom was knowing how little he knew. By asking innocent questions of so-called experts, he exposed their lack of knowledge. This was very important for philosophy and science because, after Socrates, the best thinkers questioned their assumptions before forming a theory. The most famous example is Rene Descartes' method of doubt, rejecting anything that could be doubted. His second idea was virtue and care for the soul. He said people cared for wealth and status but neglected the soul. Virtue is knowledge: whoever knows the good will do it. It is never right to do wrong, even when wronged, and he sought a universal definition of justice against Sophist relativism. Virtue is needed for true happiness, which differs from pleasure. Socrates was one of the first to seriously consider virtue, and Aristotle and the Roman Stoics took him as their starting point. Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue shows the debate continues today.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 ideas x 10 marks: idea explained (5) + influence on philosophy (5). Idea 1: Socratic ignorance - questioning experts, influence on science/philosophy, Descartes' method of doubt. Idea 2: virtue and care for soul - virtue is knowledge, universal justice vs Sophists, happiness vs pleasure, influence on Aristotle, Stoics, MacIntyre. Both ideas must be separate and clear.

rows.prompt: Present a summary of two of Plato's main ideas and explain why each was important in the development of philosophy. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Plato's first idea is the theory of ideal forms. Things in our world take their qualities from ideal forms that exist independently, such as justice, beauty or sweetness. The form is more real than the object because it never changes or decays, while physical things do - like the kilogram prototype that lost almost 50 milligrams over 130 years. In the allegory of the cave, prisoners mistake shadows for reality; the sun represents the ultimate good. This was important because Aristotle built on it, and the Neoplatonists of the third century CE revived it, influencing Christian thinkers like St Augustine. Plato's second idea is an ultimate good, the summum bonum, which brings true happiness. In the Philebus, Socrates argues against Protarchus that pure pleasure suits only an oyster; Plato's view is a mix of pleasure and wisdom led by reason. In the Phaedrus, the chariot shows reason (the charioteer) guiding appetite (dark horse) and spirit (white horse). This was important because the Neoplatonists said all things aim at this good, and Aquinas said God is the end humans direct themselves to. It also provoked opposition from Nietzsche's nihilism, while Robert Nozick supported Plato against hedonism.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 ideas x 10 marks: summary (5) + importance (5). Ideal forms: independent, unchanging, more real; IPK example; cave allegory; influence on Aristotle, Neoplatonists, Augustine. Ultimate good: summum bonum, Philebus, chariot allegory, reason; influence on Neoplatonists, Aquinas, debate with Nietzsche, Nozick.

rows.prompt: Outline two of Aristotle's main ideas and explain the importance of each in the development of philosophy. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Aristotle studied for over twenty years at Plato's Academy, but came to disagree with his teacher. His first idea was substantial forms. He did not accept that forms exist independently in an abstract way; the real object truly exists, and forms exist because we observe them in objects. A substantial form cannot be changed without the object changing its nature, while an accidental form is only on the surface. A white stone painted red has an accidental change, but if it became square, black and spongy it would be substantially different. This idea greatly influenced scholastic philosophers, especially Thomas Aquinas, and Francisco Suarez, while Descartes tried to replace it with a mechanistic view. His second idea was the first cause or unmoved mover, in his Metaphysics. Because everything changes and perishes, there must be an unchanging, immaterial cause setting everything in motion, which he called God, 'thought of thought'. God moves things by being loved as their goal, like a magnet. Unlike the Christian God, he has no plan for the world. This idea of an ordered universe refuted the Sophists' relativism, influenced Neoplatonists like Plotinus, and inspired Christian philosophers such as Aquinas.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 ideas x 10 marks: idea explained (5) + importance (5). Substantial forms: vs Plato's ideal forms; substantial vs accidental; stone example; influence on Aquinas, Suarez, Descartes' reaction; School of Athens. First cause/unmoved mover: Metaphysics, unchanging and immaterial, thought of thought, moves by being loved; differences from Christian God; refutes relativism; Plotinus, Aquinas.

rows.prompt: Identify and briefly explain three key moments in the development of philosophical thought from the classical to the contemporary period. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The first key moment was the medieval Christian philosophers. After Constantine sponsored Christianity, thinkers returned to earlier philosophy. St Augustine, influenced by Neoplatonism, taught that the physical world has a spiritual dimension and humans have free will. In Confessions he wrote, 'our hearts are restless until they rest in You'. St Thomas Aquinas combined Aristotle with Christian revelation, arguing that reason works within faith and that only God, the complete good, satisfies human desire for happiness. The second key moment was the Age of Reason in the seventeenth century. After the Humanists, the Renaissance, new astronomy, the printing press and the Reformation, thinkers relied on observation and first principles. Rene Descartes used his method of doubt, even imagining an evil demon tricking him, and concluded that he could not doubt that he was doubting: 'I think, therefore I am'. The third was Romanticism and existentialism. Rousseau and the Romantics valued passion, emotion and mystery against cold reason. Existentialism, starting with Kierkegaard, saw humans as masters of their destiny. Nietzsche declared 'God is dead', so humans must create their own values, and proposed the superman and eternal recurrence.
rows.marking_scheme: 3 moments: 6 + 7 + 7 marks. Each: moment named and dated/contextualised (2) + key thinker(s) and ideas explained (4-5). May refer to: medieval (Augustine - Manichaeism, Confessions, love; Aquinas - Aristotle, faith and reason, ultimate goal); Age of Reason (Humanism, Renaissance, Reformation, printing, Descartes, method of doubt, evil demon, Cogito); Romanticism/existentialism (Rousseau, Blake, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche - God is dead, superman, eternal recurrence).
